items.abstract: <jats:p>LLM evaluators often fail in two distinct ways: they reward persuasive but structurally invalid outputs, and they apply hardening layers in ways that shift failures rather than uniformly eliminating them. We study evaluator hardening through three mechanisms: deterministic score gates, adversarial precedent memory, and an ordering ablation that applies precedent memory only after identifying the thesis crux. We benchmark four conditions on a mixed-family suite of 10 specimens (8 bad, 2 good) and a narrower claim-test-mismatch suite of 3 historical failures. Deterministic gates reduce reward-channel corruption relative to a soft judge. Adversarial precedent memory improves default evaluator utility across repeated mixedfamily runs, primarily through lower false-accept and false-reject rates and higher mean good-specimen scores. A crux-first ablation improves detection on claim-test-mismatch failures but does not dominate on the broader suite, indicating that primitive-ordering gains are exploit-family-specific rather than uniformly dominant. Finally, the benchmark surfaced a blind spot in the evaluator itself: primitive conditioning caused a missed detection on a historical specimen, which led to a new architectural constraint and follow-up ablation. The resulting contribution is not autonomous self-improvement, but a reproducible human-in-the-loop methodology in which evaluator failures are converted into new evaluator constraints. The strongest evidence here concerns evaluator hardening, exploit-familyspecific ordering effects, and this failure-to-constraint method; we do not extend the present experiments to claims of broad out-of-distribution superiority.</jats:p>
title: Adversarial Precedent Memory: Hardening LLM Evaluators Through Mined Failure Constraints

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for primary title and abstract screening in evidence synthesis. Autonomous use, meaning an LLM that issues EXCLUDE decisions without human confirmation, depends on very high recall. Within a planned evidencesynthesis workstream whose eligibility rubric spans eight evidence families centred on clinicalguideline updating and recommendation evolution, this study specified, in dated and internally hash-locked protocol documents (prospectively specified internal documentation; this study was not publicly preregistered), a validation requirement for permitting autonomous AI screening: the exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound on the LLM’s recall for relevant records, measured against a human dual-reviewer reference standard, had to reach 95%. Objective. To determine whether one specific LLM screening configuration, frozen before Gate C execution as recorded in dated internal documentation, met this protocol-defined recall requirement on the study’s calibration frame. Methods. The evaluation used a 1,048-record stratified, relevance-enriched calibration frame, which was not a representative sample of the larger sealed search corpus of approximately 4,082 records (about 61% of the frame was an entire citation-chained methods-literature stratum, plus fixed clinical [n = 200] and legislative [n = 150] proxy draws and a fixed 60-record difficultnegative stress set). Two reviewers independently classified every frame record (INCLUDE / EXCLUDE / UNRESOLVED) against the study rubric; decision sets were hash-locked before comparison; disagreements were reconciled by documented discussion, with an unresolved disagreement recorded as UNRESOLVED (not defaulted to INCLUDE) and referred to a third reviewer. One of the two initial reviewers was the study author, so the reference standard is not fully independent of the study team. A verbatim, hash-locked prompt was then run once over the entire frame in 43 batches through the Claude Code Agent tool, a subscription-based agent interface (requested model parameter value “sonnet”; the retained execution record identifies this invocation surface but carries no independently checkable model-identity string beyond that label). Model outputs were joined to the sealed reference standard by identifier; the single UNRESOLVED record was excluded from binary denominators and reported separately. The primary outcome was recall (reference-INCLUDE records the model called INCLUDE or UNCERTAIN, both of which route to human review under the design, divided by all reference-INCLUDE records), with an exact one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound and a protocol-defined two-outcome rule (a lower bound of 95% or above meets the requirement; below 95% does not). The one-sided Clopper–Pearson lower bound was the protocol-defined decision statistic for this relevance-enriched frame and is not a confidence bound for recall in the parent corpus or in any other corpus. Specificity, falsepositive rate, raw agreement, the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), the lost-evidence quantity (reference-INCLUDE records routed to model EXCLUDE), and family-level results are descriptive secondary outcomes and are properties of this relevance-enriched frame, not corpuswide estimates. Results. Model output covered all 1,048 records (1,048 unique identifiers; no duplicates or omissions). The reference standard contained 498 INCLUDE, 549 EXCLUDE, and 1 UNRESOLVED record; pre-reconciliation reviewer agreement was 76.5% (Cohen’s kappa 0.55). Of 498 confirmedrelevant records in the frame, the frozen configuration preserved 234 for human review and routed 264 to EXCLUDE. Observed recall was 46.99% (234/498); the exact one-sided 95% Clopper– Pearson lower bound was 43.23%, against the protocol-defined 95% requirement. The requirement was not met, and this is a permanent result for this calibration run under the study’s governance rules. On this frame, 264 of 498 reference-relevant records (53.01%) were routed to model EXCLUDE (lost evidence; the complement of recall). Descriptive secondary metrics on this frame were specificity 83.42%, false-positive rate 16.58%, raw agreement 66.09%, and MCC 0.3283. Missed relevant records were concentrated: 181 of 264 (68.6%) were in one evidence family (clinical-guideline updating, implementation, comparison, and versioning), and 244 of 264 (92.4%) in that family plus the information-retrieval family. For the entity-resolution and record-linkage family, observed frame-level recall was 96.40%, with a one-sided 95% lower bound of 92.59%. A protocol-specified diagnostic analysis, conducted after the gate outcome was determined and introducing no new data, suggested that many exclusions were consistent with the narrower operational construct specified in the frozen prompt.&nbsp;</jats:p>
title: Evaluating a Frozen LLM Configuration for Clinical-Guideline Literature Screening: A Protocol-Defined Validation Study

items.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into critical infrastructure, externally auditing their safety mechanism activation without internal access becomes essential. This paper investigates whether LLM safety refusals produce a detectable computational footprint at the operating system level across multi- modal side channels. We frame this as a Safety Mechanism Activation Detection problem, employing high-resolution eBPF kernel tracing and GPU telemetry to classify model outputs as Refusal or Compliance. Initial experiments on Meta Llama 3.1 8B yielded high predictive accuracy (AUC ≥ 0.93). However, a rigorous seven-phase analysis revealed this performance was driven entirely by a confounding variable: response length. To isolate genuine safety-mechanism- activation signatures, we applied Length-Controlled Matching, retaining only response pairs with identical token counts. When response length was strictly controlled, the predictive power of kernel and GPU features collapsed to ran- dom chance (AUC ≈ 0.50), despite concurrent white-box analysis proving that the model’s internal representations clearly distinguish safety contexts (AUC 0.84-0.89). We therefore propose the Kernel Blindness hypothesis: under strictly bounded compute environments (single-GPU, 4-bit quantized, non-batched dense transformer inference), the semantic intent of neural operations is indistinguish- able at the kernel level. This phenomenon is rigorously confirmed across three major 7-8B model architectures (Llama 3.1, Gemma, and Mistral), demonstrat- ing that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) safety alignment produces no externally detectable computational signatures under these specific constraints. This overarching negative result highlights a fundamental limita- tion in black-box monitoring for edge deployments and emphasizes the need for grey-box auditing approaches.
title: The Kernel Blindness Hypothesis: Investigating OS-Level Detectability of LLM Safety Mechanisms

items.abstract: <jats:p>Attack-graph-based network hardening evaluations seldom ask whether the reported metric is the right metric or whether the increasingly common LLM reporting layer is reliable. \textsc{NetHarden} pairs a deterministic budgeted coverage-to-cost optimizer over host--vulnerability attack graphs (25 verified real CVEs from NVD) with a structured LLM remediation interface. The optimizer reaches 99.5\% mean weighted risk reduction on 30 synthetic networks and ties an LP-optimal set-cover ILP on all 130 networks (30-net plus 100-net expansion). Beyond the optimizer, a $\pm 50\%$ coefficient sensitivity sweep yields a 0.012\,pp spread, and two metric-independent attacker models (passive random-walk and adaptive Viterbi-style, the latter plan-aware) find all methods statistically indistinguishable from doing nothing, with the adaptive attacker&apos;s best-path probability identical to three decimals across seven methods on both suites. A six-model dual-judge LLM study with a 3-format prompt ablation finds every model returns a non-empty report on every plan; programmatic CVE- and host-level checks score 0.99--1.00 F1 with zero fabricated identifiers, while LLM-judge faithfulness reaches 6.21/10 with strong ordinal agreement ($\rho{=}0.875$) but zero agreement on the deployment threshold ($\kappa{=}0$). The combined evidence reframes \textsc{NetHarden} as a methodology contribution arguing for harder benchmarks and multi-objective evaluation, not a new optimizer.</jats:p>
title: NetHarden: Auditable Attack-Graph Hardening with Multi-Metric and LLM-Reliability Evaluation

items.abstract: Current AI systems can combine foundation models, retrieval, tools, agents, and execution controls, yet still amplify an unsupported premise or require repeated user correction because generation, review, and release are not organized as one bounded epistemic episode. This systems-engineering proposal translates selected functions from the human Theoretical-Mechanistic-Experiential (TME) framework into a generic artificial architecture. The source framework distinguishes the real-time experiential field from cognition, memory, and action, and orders correction through salience, attention, ordinary awareness, functional self-awareness, reflective delay, secondary segmentation, discriminative comparison, and renewed orientation. The proposed TME LLM OS retains the Transformer-foundation-model core while adding episode continuity, source provenance, role-specific agents, structured correction, residual-mismatch assessment, and gated execution. Runtime correction returns unresolved mismatch to the current episode until provisional convergence reaches a task-dependent tolerance |Δ| ≤ ε; validated corrections can enter a separate, governed, auditable, versioned, and reversible refinement path across episodes. The proposal does not equate functional implementation with lived experience. It yields testable predictions concerning grounding, recovery from false premises, safe release, recurrence of corrected errors, user burden, total task cost, and time-to-acceptable-result.
title:

items.abstract: <jats:p>Tool-using Large Language Model (LLM) agents pose a security risk that differs from text-only misuse: an unsafe response can become a harmful ac tion. This paper investigates that risk through configuration-level semantic brittleness, defined as the possibility that an agent’s safety behavior changes when operator-controlled deployment settings change, even though malicious intent remains constant. We focus on three configuration factors—system persona, prefixed conversation history, and model-facing tool definition— and develop an Adversarial Configuration Harness for structured red-teaming across model families. The empirical program uses an exploratory stage fol lowed by a frozen confirmatory stage comprising 570 trials across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen-family models. Three findings emerge: persona fram ing is the strongest factor affecting safety failure; tool-definition effects are real but family-specific in mechanism; and history effects depend on seman tic type rather than a simple safe/unsafe continuum. In the combined-factor experiment, persona produced the largest Safety Failure Rate spread (66.7 percentage points), compared with 16.7 for history and 7.5 for tool definition. The study shows that safe deployment depends not only on model choice, but also on how the surrounding configuration is presented.</jats:p>
title: Configuration-Level Semantic Brittleness in Tool-Using LLM Agents: A Factor-Ranking Study of Persona, History, and Tool Definition

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Many factories use Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) to track and manage work on the shop floor. Setting up a single MES system can take weeks. It often needs expert help. The setup process involves selecting settings, defining workflows, and connecting tools or machines. Mistakes or delays in setup can result in poor outcomes or wasted time.
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) can facilitate a more streamlined and efficient setup. The goal is to support teams by offering smart setup tips based on past work, system rules, and best practices. These tips focus on digital manufacturing, the market available tools that many factories use to run their MES.
The testing methodology utilized both structured data from MES system logs, current configurations, and previous records, and unstructured data, including work instructions, operator notes, system flow diagrams, etc. The model learned to suggest settings based on what had worked well in the past. When given a few inputs, it can now suggest complete setup plans. These can include production steps, quality checks, and machine data links.
The model also verifies if the suggested setup adheres to the rules in Digital Manufacturing. It flags problems early, so users can fix them before they go live. This helps teams avoid long delays later in the process.
To test this, we ran the tool on actual machine setups. It provided clear information and reduced setup time by almost 30%. It also helped new users get started quickly without needing extensive training. In many cases, the suggestions matched what experts would choose. The
 
 
method is not meant to replace people. It helps them move faster and avoid simple errors. Experts still review the final setup. However, with fewer manual steps, they can focus on the more challenging aspects.
The research gap lies in the fact that digital manufacturing systems still rely on manual rules. Current tools can’t process large text-based instructions or connect them to real-time MES configurations. This work addresses that gap by testing automated configuration suggestions at scale.
In short, this paper demonstrates how innovative tools can support MES setup by providing valuable insights and practical tips. We used past setups and system rules to train the tool. Early results indicate that it can save time and enable users to produce better work. This can help factories utilize the digital manufacturing solution more effectively.
Method: In this paper, we propose an Enhanced Association Rule Mining (EARM) framework for feature selection on text classification tasks. EARM's process for finding rules works at different levels, helps distinguish between specific and overall rules, enhances traditional association rule mining, uses a new method to balance support, confidence, and lift metrics, and combines different rule mining techniques to make it more reliable.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Linux kernel specialization can improve system efficiency, but configuration changes may also alter functionality, compatibility, and security. Performance gains are difficult to interpret unless the configuration that was realized and executed is established. Existing configuration-tailoring, performance-search, and LLM-assisted methods address parts of this problem separately. They do not connect workload-derived evidence, model proposals, deterministic Kconfig realization, booted-state identity, empirical performance, and deployment-policy compliance in one auditable process. Intelligent Kernel Configuration (IKC) addresses this gap through an evidence-bounded workflow. Workload traces guide candidate selection, and local Kconfig knowledge constrains LLM-assisted editing. Deterministic configuration tools establish realizable states, while boot-time configurations define experimental identity. Repeated measurements provide performance evidence, and an explicit policy gate determines deployment eligibility. Across representative web-serving, database, storage, media-processing, and scheduler workloads, IKC produced workload-dependent improvements over conventional configurations. Several workload classes retained supported advantages over machine-tailored alternatives. Evidence for the contribution of trace conditioning was more concentrated, and explicit hardening constraints preserved much of the measured performance. Complementary network-path and performance-oriented comparisons were consistent with this interpretation. These findings position model assistance within a traceable realization and validation framework, linking generated recommendations to explicit system evidence and operational outcomes. The resulting workflow establishes a reproducible foundation for workload-aware kernel specialization under well-defined operational constraints.</jats:p>
title: IKC: Auditing LLM-Assisted Linux Kernel Configuration with Workload Evidence

items.abstract: <jats:p>Urban Internet-of-Things (IoT) infrastructures increasingly host distributed artificial intelligence workloads across heterogeneous edge environments, supporting applications such as urban monitoring, resource optimization, and large-scale sensing analytics. Despite the rapid adoption of edge AI, current systems lack a unified architectural layer responsible for orchestrating distributed intelligence across dynamic urban infrastructures. Existing orchestration mechanisms are typically rule-based and rely on low-level telemetry signals such as latency, node availability, or network conditions, limiting their ability to interpret the contextual meaning of system behavior and environmental events. This paper introduces Urban AI OS, a trustworthy LLM-based semantic control layer for distributed urban edge intelligence. The proposed architecture transforms heterogeneous telemetry and environmental signals into high-level semantic events through large language model reasoning, enabling context-aware orchestration decisions including adaptive topology management, workload coordination, and node role assignment. To address the reliability risks associated with LLM-assisted control, Urban AI OS employs confidence-gated execution with deterministic fallback policies, post-action monitoring, rollback, and auditable decision logging to constrain the operational impact of uncertain or erroneous LLM recommendations. By decoupling semantic reasoning from the data plane execution of AI workloads, Urban AI OS provides a model-agnostic framework for managing large-scale urban edge intelligence infrastructures. Experimental evaluation on a real-world urban IoT deployment with 50+ edge devices demonstrates that the proposed semantic operating layer improves system responsiveness by 35%, reduces unnecessary topology changes by 42%, and improves communication efficiency compared to conventional rule-based and adaptive threshold baselines, while maintaining confidence calibration through formal fallback mechanisms.</jats:p>
title: Urban AI OS: An LLM-Driven Semantic Orchestration Layer for Distributed Edge Intelligence

items.abstract: <jats:p>Diante da crescente ubiquidade da inteligência artificial (IA), em especial os large language models (LLM), como ChatGPT, Gemini ou Claude, emerge um dilema pedagógico cuja problemática central reside na tensão entre a proficiência em tecnologias de IA para o mundo do trabalho e o impacto de sua utilização não mediada sobre a aprendizagem propedêutica. Este artigo objetiva examinar as implicações do uso do LLM no desenvolvimento do pensamento crítico, durante a formação das competências basilares no âmbito da Educação Profissional, Científica e Tecnológica (EPCT). A pesquisa caracteriza-se como estudo exploratório e descritivo, conduzido por revisão integrativa da literatura, com corpus constituído por artigos científicos indexados nas bases Scopus e Web of Science, selecionados mediante critérios de inclusão e exclusão orientados por cinco eixos temáticos. Os resultados evidenciam que a ausência de bases conceituais consolidadas leva os estudantes a aceitarem passivamente as saídas geradas pela IA, comprometendo a aprendizagem em profundidade. Os estudos demonstram que os LLM suprimem as dificuldades desejáveis que constituem o motor do desenvolvimento cognitivo, inibindo processos de assimilação, acomodação e metacognição. Evidencia-se, ainda, que, sem mediação pedagógica intencional, a IA deixa de operar como ferramenta e passa a atuar como tecnologia estruturante, alterando os fins da própria aprendizagem. Conclui-se que a variável decisiva não é a presença ou a ausência da tecnologia no itinerário formativo, mas o momento de sua inserção e a qualidade da mediação pedagógica, de modo que a integração da IA deve ser posterior à consolidação das competências basilares que alicerçam a autonomia intelectual do egresso da EPCT.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Migrating decades-old middleware estates to container platforms is dominated less by code change than by configuration translation: WebSphere resources.xml definitions for JDBC providers, data sources, and JMS activation specifications, IBM MQ object scripts in MQSC, and TIBCO BusinessWorks deployment descriptors must be re-expressed as Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, ConfigMaps, and Secret references. We report an industry-perspective empirical evaluation of large language model (LLM) assistance for this task. A reference pipeline normalises legacy sources into an intermediate configuration model, retrieves enterprise golden templates, naming rules, and approved prior translations, and subjects generated artefacts to four gates (schema validation with kubeconform, Rego policy checks, server-side dry-run, and an attribute-level fidelity diff) whose structured diagnostics drive a bounded repair loop. On a 240-artefact corpus spanning eight configuration classes, we compare zero-shot generation, zero-shot with repair, retrieval augmentation, and retrieval with repair. The combined approach raised schema validity from 71% to 98% and all-gate pass from 30% to 92%, and reduced engineer correction effort by 71% relative to manual translation. Semantic fidelity rose only from 68% to 89%, however, and validation loops improved validity far more than fidelity. Residual errors concentrated in TLS configuration, integration-runtime descriptors, and capacity-bearing pool and concurrency settings, which pass every structural check yet change runtime behaviour. We identify these classes as requiring mandatory human review and offer practitioner guidance on retrieval content, policy-guarded repair, and fidelity measurement</jats:p>
title: LLM-Assisted Translation of Legacy Middleware Configuration into Cloud-Native Deployment Artifacts: An Empirical Evaluation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Enterprises increasingly run GPU-bound workloads such as Large Language Model (LLM) inference inside virtualized infrastructure, yet practitioners have little systematic guidance on how the choice of virtualization platform affects GPU passthrough in configuration effort as much as performance. This study’s primary contribution is a structured, paired comparison of configuration complexity and performance across six platforms (Proxmox VM and LXC, native KVM, OpenStack VM and Zun, and Podman) on a single NVIDIA RTX 4500 Ada GPU, emphasizing the under-documented container paths (OpenStack Zun and Podman with the Container Device Interface). The platforms differ most in configuration complexity, where OpenStack, especially Zun, proved the most demanding and Proxmox and LXC the most straightforward. As a confirmatory baseline, for a small-model, low-concurrency vLLM workload that does not saturate the device, exclusive passthrough yields statistically equivalent throughput, duration, and inter-token latency across all platforms, within 2% of bare metal; this equivalence is bounded to the non-saturating regime tested and is not a general claim. Running two containers concurrently (each capped at 45% of GPU memory, compute time-sliced) doubled the offered load and raised aggregate throughput by 12–14%, consistent with idle GPU capacity but not isolating a GPU-sharing benefit.</jats:p>
title: GPU Passthrough Across Virtualization Platforms for LLM Inference: Configuration Complexity and a Small-Model Performance Baseline

items.abstract: <jats:p>Engineering rules often rely on dimensions copied from supplier documents. A value may look correct yet belong to another chair option, measurement object, or source that lacks a required condition. Contract-Guided Frozen-Evidence Verification (CGFEV) freezes assigned files and target configuration, while a Rule Card states what must be established. An LLM writes typed propositions and locators; deterministic Gate v0.2 controls release. We evaluated four frozen routes on commercial seating. Holdout-A contained 48 family-isolated natural cases, including 47 with binary Gold; Holdout-B contained 20 controlled pairs. On Holdout-A, B1 released 4/8 Gold-ELIGIBLE cases and falsely admitted 6/39 Gold-NOT_ELIGIBLE cases. R0, L1, and the text-only V1 prompt variant recorded no observed false admissions and released 0/8 eligible cases. R0 completed 47/47 binary cases, whereas L1 and V1 ended in ERROR on 12 and 14 cases, leaving substantive decisions for 35/47 and 33/47. Every route missed all six eligible members and all four required direction changes in Holdout-B. All 88 formal V1 records had empty visual_assets fields, so these results provide no evidence about visual or multimodal qualification. Together, these results distinguish false admission, eligible release, and execution completion as separate evaluation dimensions. CGFEV provides an auditable admission boundary for configuration-sensitive evidence qualification.</jats:p>
title: CGFEV: Auditable LLM-Assisted Qualification of Configuration-Sensitive Manufacturing Evidence for Commercial Seating Design

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as flexible resources for self-directed foreign-language learning, yet limited research explains how learners configure these systems as pedagogical partners. This study examined pedagogical role construction, modality–pedagogy alignment, affordance realization, breakdowns, and regulatory demands in learner–LLM interaction. Using a retrospective observational computational content-analysis design, 117 first-person public posts and comments, representing 80 pseudonymous participants, were analyzed from seven public forums and X. Structured multi-label coding and quantitative analyses identified eight pedagogical roles and examined relationships among interaction modalities, learning activities, perceived affordances, and breakdowns. Results showed that learners reported configuring LLMs as multifunctional pedagogical partners, most prominently as interlocutors, while 65.8% of accounts involved multiple roles. Voice interaction was significantly associated with conversation and pronunciation, whereas text was associated with vocabulary learning, supporting modality–pedagogy alignment. More orchestrated learning configurations were associated with greater perceived benefits, particularly personalization and convenience, although an apparent difference in activity breadth was substantially attenuated once the activities used to define orchestration were excluded from the count. However, 43.6% of accounts reported concerns, revealing function-specific breakdowns involving accuracy/language reliability, access/privacy/system constraints, pedagogical sustainability, interaction/continuity, and voice/technical reliability. The findings support an empirically informed framework conceptualizing learner–LLM interaction as an AI-mediated regulatory process involving role construction, modality and activity configuration, affordance realization, monitoring, breakdown detection, and regulatory demand. Psychological self-regulation and objective proficiency gains were not directly measured.</jats:p>
title: From chatbot to language-learning partner: learner–LLM configuration, affordances, and regulatory demands in foreign language learning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Firewall configuration auditing across enterprise environments remains manual and time-intensive. Commercial platforms are proprietary, expensive and provide pass or fail verdicts without Large Language Model (LLM)-driven reasoning or Security Operations Centre (SOC) integration. Published systems do not offer multi-vendor configuration retrieval, LLM-based auditing, NIST SP 800-53 mapping and SOC dispatch within a single automated pipeline. We propose Network Security Configuration Audit Tool (NSCAT), an LLM-driven methodology that normalises six-vendor configurations into a 34-field Canonical Data Model (CDM), audits them with 36 LLMs across six providers and maps every finding to the 1,014-control NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 catalogue. A Verified or AI-inferred tagging mechanism marks each finding by line-level match against its source configuration, surfacing unverifiable LLM outputs. Completed audits auto-dispatch severity-tagged alerts to Wazuh Security Information &amp; Event Management (SIEM) and email network-team reports via Shuffle Security Orchestration, Automation &amp; Response (SOAR) under auditor and operations access separation. Across 303 audits, NSCAT surfaces 2,231 unique findings with zero score-extraction failures, 99.34% PDF generation, 99.96% RAG retrieval success rate (a control returned for every finding), and 100% per-attempt SOC delivery. On a 100-finding ground truth, top-1 mapping precision (correct-control rate) is 27% strict, 39% lenient; 37.7% are Verified and 62.3% are AI-inferred (n=231, post-deployment). Median audit-to-notification latency is 21 seconds, six orders of magnitude below the 180-day PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 1.2.7 Network Security Control (NSC) review cadence. NSCAT is the first to measure NIST SP 800-53 mapping precision against ground truth and compress this cadence on open-source infrastructure.</jats:p>
title: NSCAT: LLM-Driven Firewall Configuration Auditing with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based NIST SP 800-53 Mapping and Automated Security Operations Centre Delivery

items.abstract: <jats:p>Story point estimation is widely used in agile software planning, yet automated estimation remains challenging because issue descriptions and story point distributions vary substantially across projects. This study examines configuration sensitivity and comparative performance in compact large language model (LLM)‐based story point estimation through a controlled project‐level study using five TAWOS projects and two ~1–1.5B‐parameter compact backbones with frozen parameters and trainable prediction heads. The study comprises four‐factor configuration analysis covering maximum sequence length, metadata concatenation, learning rate, and soft‐target mixing; metadata‐free sensitivity analysis; learning‐rate–soft‐target‐mixing interaction analysis; comparison with three aligned baselines; assessment of alternative temperature‐selection objectives; and computational‐cost evaluation. Soft‐target mixing and learning rate show the larger average mean absolute error (MAE) effects among the four evaluated factors, with mean high‐minus‐low effects of −0.0535 and −0.0458, respectively, although both vary in direction across project–backbone–seed scenarios. The metadata‐free analysis shows similar average effect magnitudes for learning rate and soft‐target mixing, while the interaction between these two factors is heterogeneous, with 11 negative and 9 positive scenario‐level contrasts. When compact configurations and baseline methods are selected independently using seed‐averaged validation MAE, the corresponding test results favor the compact configuration in three projects and the selected baseline in two, with additional project‐specific variation among TFIDF‐LGBM, MiniLM‐MLP, and CodeBERT‐FT. Temperature‐selection rules produce different MAE, snapped‐expected calibration error (ECE), and negative log‐likelihood (NLL) profiles. The compact configurations require very small trainable prediction heads but retain substantially higher inference latency and memory requirements than the evaluated baselines; method‐level mean raw‐text‐to‐logits latency ranges ~0.37–25.72 ms/sample in the reported NVIDIA A10 environment. Overall, the results characterize compact‐LLM story point estimation by heterogeneous configuration sensitivity, project‐dependent model ranking, and accuracy–cost trade‐offs rather than a single consistently preferable configuration or model family.</jats:p>
title: Configuration Factors for Compact LLM‐Based Story Point Estimation: A Controlled Project‐Level Empirical Study

                  <jats:p>Rapid fault self‐restoration in complex power distribution networks is crucial. Edge Computing Units (ECUs) offer decentralized control, but their optimal configuration is challenging. This paper proposes a Large Language Model (LLM) enhanced Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) framework for ECU configuration, explicitly considering advanced wireless communication (e.g., 5G/6G, LoRa) characteristics. The LLM aids in intelligent population initialization and adaptive particle guidance within PSO. This approach aims to optimize ECU placement and inter‐ECU data exchange. Simulations on IEEE test systems show that the LLM‐enhanced PSO significantly improves ECU configurations, reduces communication delays, and enhances self‐restoration performance, thereby bolstering smart grid resilience.</jats:p>
